Article Title: Shoulder surgery, 7 months out, one unforgettable throw: How Yash Vir Singh won CWG bronze
Article Text:
Yash Vir Singh

Before Glasgow glory came years of struggle

Yash Vir Singh (Special Arrangements)

The father who never gave up on Yash Vir

Yash Vir Singh with his father (Special Arrangements)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Before Yash Vir Singh walked up for his sixth and final throw in the men's javelin final at Scotstoun Stadium, two voices stayed with him.One came from Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra."You're throwing well. Just keep it straight and believe in yourself. It's your last throw, just make sure you don't foul. You can do it."The other came from his father and coach, Rai Singh."It's the last throw. Put everything into it."Seconds later, the javelin landed at 85.41 metres.Yash Vir leapt from seventh place to the bronze medal position, registering a personal best by almost three metres. The effort not only earned him a place on the podium alongside Neeraj Chopra, who took silver behind Sri Lanka's Rumesh Tharanga, but also made him only the third Indian to win a Commonwealth Games medal in men's javelin. For the first time in the history of the event, two Indians shared the Commonwealth Games podium.The medal came in one of the strongest men's javelin fields assembled at a Commonwealth Games.The Glasgow final featured one of the strongest javelin fields assembled at a Commonwealth Games. Besides Neeraj and Yash Vir, India also had Rohit Yadav in the final. Reigning Commonwealth Games champion Arshad Nadeem was back to defend his title.Former world champion Anderson Peters of Grenada, Trinidad and Tobago's Keshorn Walcott and former Commonwealth champion Julius Yego were all in the fray. Rumesh Tharanga, meanwhile, arrived in Glasgow after a series of impressive performances and eventually walked away with gold.For much of the evening, Yash Vir remained in the background.Having squeezed into the final in 10th place during qualification, few would have backed the Indian Railways ticket collector to leave Glasgow with a medal. His best throw heading into the final round measured 81.33m, leaving him seventh in the standings with one attempt remaining.Then came his final attempt."I'd made up my mind - today it was do or die. I shouted it out and then went for the throw. It wasn't easy. I'd already committed two fouls and even my fifth throw was only 76.95 metres. My only thought was to produce my personal best. I had nothing to lose. But there was a hunger built up over the last four years. I'll always remember that 85.41m throw. I'm immensely grateful to God," Yash Vir told TimesofIndia.com.The conditions hardly made life easier. Several leading throwers struggled to find consistency as gusty conditions made it difficult to judge the release. Yash Vir adjusted quickly."I quickly calculated the wind conditions. Then I increased my speed a bit and made a slight change to my technique according to the wind pressure. The plan was simple - release the javelin with full power. That's it. The plan worked. I'm happy that I finally crossed the 85-metre mark. My previous best was over 83 metres at the Inter State Championships."The bronze medal was the culmination of four years spent fighting through injury, surgery and rehabilitation, all while holding on to a promise he had made to himself."Main wapsi karke dikhaunga.[I'll make a comeback]."The promise was made in 2022.During a training session, Yash Vir injured his shoulder. The damage was serious. One of the muscles in his rotator cuff - the supraspinatus - had been affected, leaving him in constant pain and eventually requiring surgery at the Abhinav Bindra Targeting Performance (ABTP) Centre in Jaipur.The operation was successful, but it came with another challenge. Doctors ruled him out of competition for at least seven months. For an athlete whose life revolved around throwing the javelin, the rehabilitation was as much a mental battle as a physical one."It was an extremely difficult time. All I wanted was to return to the field," Yash Vir said."The surgery went well and my treatment was completed successfully. Dr Harshvardhan Singh and Dr Aditi Thakur are like God to me. They gave me the confidence that I would be able to throw the javelin again the way I always had. Today, I am here because of them. I owe them a lot."Unable to train, he spent months confined to bed. There was little he could do physically, so he tried to stay connected with the sport in every way possible. He watched videos of his old competitions, relived some of his best throws and immersed himself in motivational books, refusing to let the dream of competing again fade away.When he eventually returned in 2023, the signs were encouraging. His comeback competition ended with a silver medal. Strong performances followed over the next two seasons, eventually earning him a place in India's squad for the Commonwealth Games.Yet, despite steady progress, Yash Vir travelled to Glasgow with little fanfare.The spotlight naturally remained on Chopra, India's Olympic and world champion, while Rohit Yadav completed the three-member Indian contingent. Yash Vir entered the competition as an outsider, having qualified for the final in 10th place.Throughout the journey, one person remained at the centre of it all - his father, Rai Singh."Now, I don't want to look back. A Commonwealth Games medal means a lot to me. You can say this is just the beginning," he said.Behind that journey has been one constant figure. His father. Rai Singh is much more than Yash Vir's coach.A former national-level javelin thrower himself, Rai won multiple national medals and Railway championship titles before becoming an athletics coach with the Indian Railways. An NIS Diploma holder, he has guided his son's career from the very beginning, overseeing not just his technique but every aspect of his routine.Long before international medals entered the conversation, father and son spent countless hours training at the Railway Ground near Jaipur railway station.The first javelin wasn't even made of metal. It was bamboo."My father is very strict. He believes in discipline. He takes care of my training, schedule, diet and every single aspect of my life. I may be his son, but he is even stricter with me than anyone else," Yash Vir said."Whatever I am today is because of him. Foreign coaches come and go after a while, but it is my father who has taught me everything from the very beginning."Even now, the technical discussions happen at home."I don't know much about biomechanics. My father understands it really well. Whatever plan he gives me, whether it's about intensity, power, run-up or the release angle, everything comes from him."At Scotstoun Stadium, Rai Singh watched from above the runway, shouting instructions after every attempt. He had never received the opportunity to compete on one of athletics' biggest stages himself.On Saturday evening in Glasgow, he watched his son stand on the Commonwealth Games podium with a bronze medal around his neck. For Yash Vir, the medal represented a personal best, a national milestone and the fulfilment of a promise he had made to himself four years ago.
Article Summary: Yash Vir Singh wins bronze in the men's javelin at the Commonwealth Games. He is the third Indian to win a Commonwealth Games medal in the event. Sri Lanka's Rumesh Tharanga won gold and India's Neeraj Chopra took silver.

Article Title: Glasgow done, all eyes on 'Amdavad 2030': India's campaign offers both promise and warning signs
Article Text:
Indian boxer Jaismine Lamboria and other athletes during the closing ceremony of the CWG 2026. (PTI Photo)

Athletics leads the way



Boxers make a statement



Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Judokas earn their place in the spotlight



PUNE: The Glasgow Commonwealth Games are over. The baton passes to India for the Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad, dubbed ‘Amdavad 2030’. With the event returning home after 20 years, India will be aiming not only to stage a better Games than Delhi 2010 but also to improve on its best-ever medal haul. At the 2010 Delhi Games, India won a record 101 medals to finish second in the overall standings.For Indian sport, Glasgow offered a mixed picture. The 39 medals collected this time were fewer than the 61 in Birmingham 2022, 66 in Gold Coast 2018 and 64 in Glasgow 2014. More importantly, those medals came from just six sports. By contrast, India’s medals had come from 17 sports in 2010, 11 in 2014, 15 in 2018 and 13 in 2022.The explanation lies partly in the programme itself. Glasgow did not include sports where India has traditionally been strong. India has won 135 medals in shooting between 1966 and 2018, excluding the 1970 Edinburgh edition. Wrestling has fetched India 114 medals across 18 editions since 1934. Yet Glasgow had no shooting, wrestling, hockey, badminton, archery or table tennis, which together had contributed 67 medals for India in Delhi 2010.As India prepares to host in 2030, the focus will be on retaining the positives from Glasgow while also bringing back its strongest disciplines.Athletics emerged as the biggest winner for India, with medals in the men’s 10,000m and 5,000m long jump, decathlon, high jump, triple jump and para-athletics adding up to 16 medals. What stood out most was the history made by Gulveer Singh, who won silver in the 10,000m and bronze in the 5,000m and Tejaswin Shankar, who claimed decathlon bronze.Yash Vir Singh also broke new ground by winning a javelin bronze in a field featuring Olympic and world champions, as well as world leaders and record holders. The para-athletes contributed three gold, two silver and one bronze, even as the 4x400m relay team had to settle for sixth place.“The performance was way better than expected. This has been a good result and it will only improve in the years to come. The result reflects the policies that the Athletics Federation of India (AFI) has adopted in the past few years,” former World Championships bronze medallist and current AFI senior vice-president Anju Bobby George told TOI.“Now we plan the training programme according to individual athletes’ requirements rather than designing a blanket programme for everyone. Some athletes train in the USA, some in Europe, because that is what best suits their future. The results are definitely going to improve in 2030 and beyond, as we also plan to host the Olympics,” she added.Boxing also delivered strongly, with seven gold among the 13 medals won. While the level of competition at the Commonwealth Games is not as demanding as at the Asian Games or Olympics, the performances will still provide a valuable confidence boost.“It is not as if these were the only medals our boxers have won so far. We had world champions, an Olympic medallist and Asian Games and Asian Championships winners at the Glasgow CWG. The field may not have been as strong as the Asiad, but it was not weak either.A good show at a competition like this gives a boost to the boxers,” 2008 Beijing Olympics bronze medallist Vijender Singh told TOI.With two historic gold and three medals overall, Indian judokas Asmita Dey, Harsh Singh and Yamini Mourya also deserve special mention. A sport that has often struggled for attention in the past appears to be finding its footing.If judo can continue on this trajectory, the possibilities are immense. With 15 medal events at the Olympics and proper investment and a cleaner administrative setup, India has genuine medal potential at the world level too.
Article Summary: Athletics emerged as the biggest winner for India, with medals in the men’s 10,000m and 5,000M long jump, decathlon, high jump, triple jump and para- athletics adding up to 16 medals. Boxing also delivered strongly, with seven gold among the 13 medals won. Judo also deserves special mention, with two historic gold and three medals overall.

Article Title: PCB appoint Michael Smith as batting coach ahead of England series on two-year deal
Article Text:
Michael Smith (Image: X)

Pakistan look to fix long-standing batting woes



Batting collapses continue to haunt Pakistan

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pakistan tour of England

Pakistan have officially appointed former South Africa first-class cricketer and coach Michael Smith as the batting coach of the men's national team, with the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) confirming the appointment on Tuesday.The 46-year-old has been handed a two-year contract and will oversee Pakistan's batting across both the red-ball and white-ball formats. Smith is set to begin his tenure ahead of Pakistan's three-match Test series against England, which starts on August 19.A Level 4 qualified coach, Smith enjoyed a decade-long playing career between 2003 and 2013, featuring in 89 first-class matches, 72 List A games and 16 T20s. He brings extensive coaching experience, having worked in the Pakistan Super League (PSL) with Islamabad United, Karachi Kings and Multan Sultans. His coaching résumé also includes stints as batting coach with Australia's Hobart Hurricanes and Cricket Tasmania, while he has also served as a coaching consultant for South Africa's KZN Inland and Eastern Province.Smith's appointment comes at a crucial time as Pakistan seek to address their recurring batting failures, particularly in pressure situations across formats. The national team has not had a full-time batting coach in recent times, with national selector Asad Shafiq occasionally stepping into the role.Meanwhile, former fast bowler Umar Gul continues as the team's bowling coach. Pakistan sit ninth in the ICC World Test Championship standings.Pakistan are currently touring the West Indies for a two-match Test series and are already trailing 0-1 after suffering a 90-run defeat in the opening Test. Despite being well placed at 244/3 in the first innings, they lost their final seven wickets for just 38 runs, before being bowled out for 120 while chasing 211 in the fourth innings.The second Test is already underway, and at stumps on Day 2, Pakistan were 76 runs behind with eight wickets in hand, still battling to level the series.Pakistan's fragile batting has become a recurring concern in recent years. Their inability to capitalise on strong positions has contributed significantly to a poor run in the longest format, with the team losing 13 of their last 17 Tests.The Pakistan men's cricket team is scheduled to tour England from August 19 to September 13, 2026, to play a three-match Test series. The matches form an integral part of the 2025–2027 ICC World Test Championship. Pakistan is currently concluding a red-ball tour in the West Indies and will arrive in England later this month, armed with newly appointed long-term batting coach Michael Smith to fix recent batting form issues.
Article Summary: Former South Africa first-class cricketer Michael Smith appointed batting coach. The 46-year-old has been handed a two-year contract and will oversee Pakistan's batting across both the red-ball and white-ball formats. Smith is set to begin his tenure ahead of Pakistan's three-match Test series against England, which starts on August 19. Pakistan are currently touring the West Indies and are already trailing 0-1.

Article Title: 'Shutdown a board decision, will honour players' contracts': Tata Steel on Jamshedpur FC shutdown
Article Text:
Jamshedpur FC players (Pic credit: Jamshedpur FC)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

KOLKATA: Even as an online petition was started by fans all over the country to save Jamshedpur FC and appeals to save the club kept growing louder, Tata Steel vice-president clarified in a news conference in Jamshedpur on Monday that the decision was entirely that of the Tata Steel board and the company will fulfil the players’ current contracts.“The decision is entirely Tata Steel board’s and has no connection of any kind with any financial irregularity or discrepancy,” Tata Steel vice-president (corporate services), DB Sundar Ramam said.“Players will receive full payment as per their contract. Besides this, Tata Steel will also try to ensure that these players can get opportunities to play in other clubs, so that their careers are not adversely affected in any way.”Sundar Ramam said the aim of the company was never to earn profit in sports but to “provide opportunities to players, promote sports culture and prepare future talent” and that was the philosophy with which it operated Jamshedpur FC over the years.“Tata Steel invested about Rs 30 to 35 crore annually in the club’s operations, and, with the support of other sponsors, about Rs 320 crore has been invested in the club so far.In the last 9 years, JFC made many accomplishments and Tata Steel is proud of this entire journey,” he added.He also added that the aim of the company will remain on grassroots development.“The closure of JFC’s operations does not mean that football will end in Jamshedpur. Tata Steel will continue to provide every possible support in the city for football competitions, local clubs, training programmes and young players,” he said while adding that Jamshedpur’s rich football tradition will continue and new talents will keep getting opportunities to move forward.
Article Summary: Tata Steel vice-president DB Sundar Ramam said the decision was entirely that of the Tata Steel board and the company will fulfil the players’ current contracts. He added that the company was never to earn profit in sports but to “provide opportunities to players, promote sports culture and prepare future talent”

Article Title: Brazil game can't mask Indian football's crisis: Bhutia says 'timing of the match is a problem'
Article Text:
Bhaichung Bhutia (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The announcement of a glamour friendly between India and Brazil should have been a moment of celebration for Indian football. Instead, it has exposed the widening gap between spectacle and substance, prompting former India captain Bhaichung Bhutia to question both the timing and the purpose of the high-profile fixture.“The timing of the Brazil friendly is a problem for me,” Bhutia said, pointing out that India will be involved in the FIFA ASEAN Cup around the same period. “The FIFA ASEAN Cup will be taking place at that time and we don’t know how the national team will be formed.” His concerns are difficult to dismiss. India, ranked 138th in the world, have been drawn alongside Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore in the ASEAN Cup, a tournament where only the group winner advances.With qualification already a challenging prospect, diverting attention towards an exhibition match raises legitimate questions about priorities. Bhutia’s criticism goes beyond scheduling. For him, the Brazil match has become a symbol of a football ecosystem struggling to address its fundamental problems.“I was wondering about the purpose of the friendly match against Brazil. Is Indian football going to gain anything out of it?” he asked.The question strikes at the heart of the debate. A match against five-time world champions Brazil will undoubtedly generate excitement, television audiences and commercial interest. But can a single evening against one of football’s global giants compensate for years of structural decline? The former captain believes it cannot. “A big corporate group like the Tatas have declared shutting down of Jamshedpur FC. It goes to show the health of Indian football,” he said.The uncertainty surrounding Jamshedpur FC has only amplified concerns about the financial sustainability of Indian football. At a time when clubs are struggling, developmental pathways remain weak and investment is shrinking, a marquee international fixture risks appearing disconnected from the realities on the ground.Bhutia painted an even bleaker picture of the current state of the game. “The focus of the football federation should be getting the house in order. Let alone the seniors, even the U-17s are failing to earn qualification in continental tournaments,” he said. “The national league is in disarray, the junior programme is rudderless and there is no money to develop the grassroots game.”His views have found support within the playing community. India full-back Nikhil Poojary echoed similar concerns on social media, noting the contrast between celebrating Brazil’s visit and waking up to news of another club shutting down operations.India has hosted football royalty before. Uruguay and Argentina played in the Nehru Cup during the 1980s, while Lionel Messi’s Argentina visited in 2011 and again in 2025. Those occasions generated excitement and memories, but they did little to alter the trajectory of Indian football.
Article Summary: Bhaichung Bhutia questions the purpose of India's friendly against Brazil. Former India captain also questions the timing of the fixture. India will also be taking part in the FIFA ASEAN Cup at the same time. BhUTia believes the Brazil match is a symbol of Indian football's problems.

Article Title: Military personnel bag 46% of India’s medals at CWG 2026
Article Text:
India's Jaismine Lamboria celebrates after winning the women's 57kg boxing final. (AP Photo)

NEW DELHI: Indian military personnel contributed the lion’s share in the country’s CWG medals tally. The Indian Army won 16 medals of India’s total haul of 39. Two Indian Navy personnel also won medals.If the medals won by Army and Navy personnel are combined, the services personnel bagged 18 medals out of the total 39, which is equivalent to 46% contribution of the services in winning medals.“A contingent of 20 Indian Army athletes won 16 medals”, the Army said, adding out of 16 medals, eight are gold, seven silver and one bronze.Praising its personnel, the Indian Army, in a post X on Monday, said, “Har kaam, desh ke naam. General Dhiraj Seth, COAS and All Ranks of Indian Army extend heartiest congratulations to the Indian Army athletes for their outstanding performance.”
Article Summary: The Indian Army won 16 medals of India’s total haul of 39. Two Indian Navy personnel also won medals. If the medals won by Army and Navy personnel are combined, the services personnel bagged 18 medals out of the total 39.

Article Title: 'Today is a happy day': Brij Bhushan Singh's first reaction after acquittal in sexual harassment case
Article Text:
Brij Bhushan Singh (PTI Photo)

Delhi court acquits Brij Bhushan Singh and Vinod Tomar

Trial followed nationwide protests

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Former Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) chief Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh on Monday welcomed the Delhi court's decision acquitting him in the sexual harassment case involving women wrestlers, describing it as a "happy day" for himself and his supporters while saying he would wait for the detailed judgment before commenting further.A Delhi court acquitted Singh and former WFI assistant secretary Vinod Tomar in the high-profile case that had dominated Indian wrestling for more than two years and sparked nationwide protests by some of the country's top wrestlers.Speaking to reporters shortly after the verdict, Singh reiterated the stand he had maintained since the allegations first surfaced."On the first day, when my first statement came, I had said that if any verdict or any charge is proven, I will hang myself. Today, the court acquitted me with honour. It is a matter of joy for me and my supporters... Today is a happy day," Singh said.He also thanked his legal team for their efforts and said he would wait for the court's detailed order before making any further comments on the case.Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate (ACJM) Ashwani Panwar of the Rouse Avenue Court pronounced the verdict, acquitting both Singh and former WFI assistant secretary Vinod Tomar.The proceedings were held in a closed courtroom after the court had reserved its judgment following the completion of final arguments by both the prosecution and defence.The case arose from allegations made by six women wrestlers, who accused Singh of sexual harassment during his tenure as WFI president.Following the complaints and protests by leading wrestlers at Delhi's Jantar Mantar in 2023, the Delhi Police registered an FIR and later filed a 1,500-page chargesheet against Singh.The chargesheet invoked Sections 354 (assault or criminal force to outrage a woman's modesty), 354A (sexual harassment), 354D (stalking) and 506(1) (criminal intimidation) of the Indian Penal Code.Tomar was named as a co-accused and faced allegations of criminal intimidation.The case became one of the biggest controversies in Indian sport, with several prominent wrestlers demanding action against Singh and staging prolonged protests in the national capital.In May 2024, the trial court framed charges against Singh for offences under Sections 354 and 354A of the IPC in connection with allegations made by five women wrestlers. Charges under Section 506(1) relating to criminal intimidation were also framed based on complaints by two wrestlers.Tomar was also charged with criminal intimidation for allegedly threatening one of the complainants.During the trial, the court heard detailed submissions from both sides. The court also examined members of the Special Investigation Team (SIT), including the investigating officer.A separate case under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act involving a minor wrestler had earlier been closed after the complainant withdrew her allegations, following which the Delhi Police filed a cancellation report.
Article Summary: Delhi court acquits Brij Bhushan Singh and Vinod Tomar in sexual harassment case. Former Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) chief described it as a "happy day" for himself and his supporters. Case arose from allegations made by six women wrestlers, who accused Singh of sexual harassment.

Article Title: Durand Cup: Doley hat-trick keeps Raengdai's fairytale alive as debutants edge TRAU in seven-goal Manipur derby
Article Text:
FC Raengdai players celebrate. (Pic Credit: Durand Cup Media)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

There seems to be no stopping FC Raengdai! After making a historic winning debut in Durand Cup, the newest football sensation from Manipur continued their run, this time with a thrilling 4-3 win over TRAU FC in a much-anticipated Manipur derby on Monday.Before the packed crowd at Khuman Lampak Main Stadium in Imphal, Mridul Doley headed in a corner kick in the 79th minute to complete his hat-trick and help Raengdai edge TRAU and stay on their fairytale journey in football.The win took the debutants to top of Group D with six points from two matches, a start few would have predicted a week earlier. NEROCA sit second on one point from a single outing, with TRAU third, also on one point but in two games. Indian Navy occupy the fourth spot without a win to their name.Reangdai attacker Doley, who had provided the assist in the solitary goal that won them the game against Indian Navy, was the star from early on, scoring on either side of the half-hour to give Raengdai a comfortable lead.TRAU’s response arrived just before the interval through Chanam Akash Meitei, only for Chongtham Kishan Singh to restore the two-goal lead in first-half stoppage time.Afdal Varikkodan pulled one back within two minutes of the restart, and when Lanchungrei Pamei turned the ball into his own net in the 67th minute, parity had been restored for the second time on the day.However, Doley had the final word, completing a memorable hat-trick to send Raengdai in lead again, this time till the final whistle.Earlier, FC1 marked their Durand Cup debut with a spirited 2-1 comeback victory over Karbi Anglong Morning Star FC in a Group F fixture at Indira Gandhi Athletic Stadium in Guwahati on Monday.Meanwhile, another debutants Langsning FC produced a sensational second-half display to cruise to a commanding 5-0 victory over Mumbay FC in a Group E fixture at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium in Shillong on the day.
Article Summary: FC Raengdai beat TRAU FC 4-3 in a much-anticipated Manipur derby on Monday. Mridul Doley scored a hat-trick to help the debutants top Group D. Earlier, FC1 marked their Durand Cup debut with a spirited 2-1 comeback victory over Karbi Anglong Morning Star FC.

Article Title: Wrestlers to challenge Brij Bhushan's acquittal; Vinesh, Bajrang say 'legal battle far from over'
Article Text:
Vinesh Phogat and Brij Bhushan Saran Singh (IANS Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Refusing to accept the trial court’s verdict, Vinesh Phogat on Monday said she and the other women wrestlers who accused former Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) chief Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh of sexual harassment will challenge his acquittal before a higher court.Vinesh, who had publicly identified herself as one of the six complainants in the case, said the wrestlers have instructed their legal team to file an appeal at the earliest. Olympic medallist Bajrang Punia reiterated that their fight for justice would continue.Their decision came after additional chief judicial magistrate Ashwini Panwar of Delhi’s Rouse Avenue Court acquitted Brij Bhushan and former WFI assistant secretary Vinod Tomar in the 2023 sexual harassment case. According to the defence, the court found the evidence insufficient and noted inconsistencies and contradictions in witness testimonies before acquitting the two accused.Reacting to the verdict, Vinesh and Bajrang issued a joint statement on social media, saying the wrestlers’ legal battle was far from over.“We are deeply saddened that the court did not find Brij Bhushan guilty of the allegations of sexual harassment made by the women wrestlers.The women wrestlers have instructed their lawyers to appeal against this decision, and the appeal will be filed as soon as possible. We have not lost hope, and the wrestlers will continue their fight,” the statement said.The two also alleged that the complainants had faced sustained pressure throughout the case.“We had to gather a lot of courage to come out onto the streets and get an FIR registered against a powerful leader of the ruling party. Using his influence and political power, Brij Bhushan intimidated several girls into withdrawing their names. However, many women wrestlers stood firm and continued fighting against him in court,” they added.Vinesh had earlier chosen to publicly identify herself as one of the six women wrestlers who filed sexual harassment complaints against Brij Bhushan despite the anonymity generally maintained in such cases, citing the extraordinary circumstances surrounding the case and the pressure faced by the women wrestlers.The allegations against Brij Bhushan surfaced in 2023, triggering one of the biggest athlete-led protests in Indian sport. Vinesh, Bajrang, Rio Olympics bronze medallist Sakshi Malik and several other wrestlers staged a 36-day sit-in at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, demanding action against the then WFI chief over allegations of sexual harassment and intimidation. The protest eventually led to the Delhi Police registering an FIR and filing a chargesheet against Brij Bhushan under relevant IPC provisions. Tomar was also chargesheeted.In May 2024, the trial court framed charges against Brij Bhushan. Proceedings thereafter continued in camera, with final arguments concluding on July 2 this year. The court delivered its verdict on Monday, acquitting both Brij Bhushan and Tomar.Welcoming the judgment, Brij Bhushan said, “I said on the very first day that if the allegations are true, I will hang myself. I am very happy that I have been acquitted today. This is good news for me and my supporters.”He added, “This case has proved that even Olympians and Olympic medal winners can lie for their own interests. This is the victory of those players and supporters who had faith in me.”WFI presidentSanjay Singh also hailed the verdict. “On behalf of the Indian wrestling fraternity, we welcome this decision. These allegations caused significant damage to wrestling. This was politically motivated,” he said.Senior advocate Rebecca John, who represented four of the six complainants, described the acquittal as “deeply, deeply disturbing”. Speaking to PTI, she questioned claims made by the defence regarding the basis of the verdict, pointing out that the detailed judgment was yet to be made available. She added that the prosecution had argued any inconsistencies in witness testimonies which she cited were minor and did not undermine the credibility of the complainants.With the trial court proceedings now over, the case is set to move to the appellate stage, with the wrestlers expected to file their appeal before a higher court in the coming days.
Article Summary: Vinesh Phogat says she and other women wrestlers will challenge acquittal of Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh. Olympic medallist Bajrang Punia reiterated that their fight for justice would continue. Vinesh had publicly identified herself as one of the six complainants in the case.

Article Title: CWG 2026: Relay flop raises Asian Games alarm
Article Text:
Vishal TK (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: Even as India celebrated a strong athletics campaign at the Commonwealth Games — highlighted by three para athletics gold medals to go with five silver and five bronze from the able-bodied contingent — attention has now shifted to the disappointing performance of the mixed 4x400m relay team.The quartet, which made the cut after surviving a rigorous selection process that saw the Athletics Federation of India (AFI) reject all the other relay combinations, failed to deliver on the biggest stage.Vishal TK, who set a national record this season with a personal best of 44.98 seconds in May, clocked a below-par 46.1 in the opening lap in the final. Ansa Babu then struggled to match the quality of the field, clocking 54.1 while rivals, led by Jamaica’s Leah Anderson (50.8 seconds), comfortably ran under 52 seconds.Santosh Kumar Tamilarasan (46.4 seconds) and Rashdeep Kaur (53.72 seconds) were unable to change the complexion of the race as India finished sixth and last in the final rankings after Australia was disqualified and Zambia failed to finish.“It seems India’s top runners peaked too early this season. Rajesh ran 45.26 in March but his performance dipped in Glasgow. Rajesh is one of our key relay runners and, with Mohammed Anas and Amoj Jacob still recovering from injuries, he is now the most experienced member of the squad.It will take a miracle for our relay runners to improve enough before the Asian Games next month,” another coach said.Rajesh, who clocked 47.00 seconds in the heats, was replaced by Santosh for the final. Several coaches who monitored the team’s preparations also questioned whether the expertise of foreign coach Jason Alexander Dawson was being fully utilised.“Two coaches training two separate groups of athletes simply doesn’t work. Whoever can’t cope with Jason’s workload shifts to the Indian coach. Ideally, all the 400m runners should train under one programme and one brain,” one coach said, referring to the parallel coaching setup under Dawson and Raj Mohan in Thiruvananthapuram.A former national coach, who had previously handled the relay squad, urged patience. “You can’t call Vishal a sub-45 runner unless he consistently runs below 45 seconds. I’m optimistic our relay squads will bounce back and perform well at the Asian Games. Earlier, India was stronger in the women’s 4x400m relay, but now the men’s team has become more competitive,” he said.Meanwhile, AFI has reportedly decided not to field the men’s 4x100m relay team at the Asian Games while clearing the remaining relay squads.
Article Summary: The mixed 4x400m relay team failed to deliver on the biggest stage. Article Title: Forging champions in Olive Green: How the Army Sports Institute has become India’s premier high performance centre
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: The resounding success of Indian Army athletes at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow is far more than a medal-winning campaign—it is the culmination of years of scientific planning, relentless discipline and institutional excellence. At the heart of this success stands the Army Sports Institute (ASI), Pune, India’s premier military high performance centre, which has once again demonstrated why it is regarded as one of the country’s finest centres for elite athlete development.With Army boxers contributing an extraordinary haul of 8 medals at the CWG, ASI’s contribution to Indian boxing has reached unprecedented heights. From Olympic hopefuls to Commonwealth champions, the institute continues to produce athletes capable of competing—and winning—against the very best in the world.Established in 2005, the Army Sports Institute was envisioned as the Indian Army ’s flagship project to identify, nurture and develop sporting excellence. Twenty-five years later, that vision has evolved into one of the country’s most successful high-performance ecosystems.Unlike conventional training centres, ASI integrates every aspect of athlete development under one roof. Elite coaching, sports science, strength and conditioning, biomechanics, nutrition, psychology, physiotherapy, recovery management and performance analytics operate seamlessly to maximise every athlete’s potential.This holistic approach has transformed ASI into a benchmark for high-performance sport in India.Boxing has emerged as one of ASI’s greatest success stories.The institute’s talent identification programme scouts promising youngsters from across India and systematically develops them through the Boys and Girls Sports Companies before transitioning the best performers into elite national-level competitors.The results are unmistakable.At Glasgow 2026, Army boxers dominated the competition, winning medals across multiple weight categories and forming the backbone of India’s historic boxing campaign. Their performances reflected exceptional technical preparation, tactical maturity and the mental resilience that are hallmarks of Army training. India’s boxing team produced its best-ever CWG performance with seven gold and three silver medals overall, underscoring the depth of the programme.Success at ASI is not accidental.Every training session is data-driven. Athlete workloads are scientifically monitored. Recovery protocols minimise injury risk. Nutrition plans are customised. Performance is analysed through modern sports science and technology.This integrated approach ensures that athletes peak when it matters most—at international championships.Equally important is the military ethos that defines every athlete trained at ASI: discipline, resilience, teamwork and the determination to perform under pressure.While boxing has become a flagship discipline, ASI’s excellence extends across athletics, wrestling, weightlifting, diving, fencing, archery and several Olympic sports.While boxing led the Army Sports Institute’s remarkable CWG campaign, its excellence extended well beyond the ring. Army athletes scripted history in athletics with a series of landmark performances. Naib Subedar Gulveer Singh became the first Indian ever to win a silver medal in the men’s 10,000m and followed it with a historic bronze in the 5,000m—the first medal by an Indian in the event at the Commonwealth Games. In doing so, he also became the first Indian track and field athlete to win two medals at a single CWG.Adding to the historic achievements, Naib Subedar Sarvesh Kushare won the silver medal in High Jump, marking India’s first-ever CWG medal in the men’s high jump. In the weightlifting arena Hav Ajaya Babu won a silver medal and created a new record in Snatch category. Together, these breakthrough performances reaffirm that the Army Sports Institute is not merely producing champions in one discipline but is emerging as India’s most successful multi-sport high-performance centre, consistently delivering athletes capable of rewriting the nation’s sporting history.The institute has consistently produced Olympians, Asian Games medallists, CWG champions and national record holders. Many of India’s finest sporting achievements over the past decade have carried the unmistakable imprint of the Army Sports Institute.As India intensifies its preparations for future Olympic Games, the Army Sports Institute provides a proven blueprint for sustained international success.Its combination of early talent identification, world-class coaching, cutting-edge sports science and unwavering institutional support has created a system capable of producing champions year after year.The Glasgow CWG have once again reaffirmed an enduring truth: when India celebrates sporting excellence, the Army Sports Institute is often at the heart of that success.From nurturing young talent to producing Commonwealth champions, ASI continues to live its motto—transforming potential into podium finishes and inspiring a new generation of athletes to wear the Tricolour with pride.The remarkable contribution of Army athletes at Glasgow is not merely a medal tally; it is a testament to twenty-five years of vision, investment and unwavering commitment to sporting excellence. Champions are not born overnight—they are forged in Olive Green.

Sai Kishore has opened up for the first time about why he featured in only three matches for Gujarat Titans during IPL 2026, saying he rushed his comeback from finger surgery and returned to competitive cricket before regaining full rhythm.The left-arm spinner had enjoyed one of the best phases of his career in 2025. He finished IPL 2025 with 19 wickets, becoming one of GT's key bowlers.But IPL 2026 turned out very differently. Sai Kishore played only three matches, bowled in just two of them and picked up one wicket as Gujarat Titans reached the final.The setback, however, had begun months before the IPL. Sai Kishore injured the ring finger of his bowling hand during a club match in Chennai in August 2025. The injury required minor surgery, but he returned to action on November 1, playing for Tamil Nadu against Vidarbha in the Ranji Trophy.The spinner, who made his India debut at the Asian Games in Hangzhou, has not played for the national team since 2023. While he had become a regular member of Gujarat Titans' squad, IPL 2026 saw him fall down the pecking order.Looking back, Sai Kishore admitted he came back too early."I think on hindsight when I reflect, more than anything, I should have given myself more time to come back to cricket from my surgery," Sai Kishore tells Cricbuzz."In the domestic season, especially till the end of Vijay Hazare, I was still getting to my full fitness. I think I shouldn't have done it at that time."He said returning before reaching full fitness affected his performances. During the same period, Rajasthan spinner Manav Suthar impressed and moved ahead of Sai Kishore in Gujarat Titans' plans. Suthar also went on to play Test cricket for India.Sai Kishore admitted the decision to return early came from the desire to get back on the field as quickly as possible."But we always get such understandings on hindsight. When we get injured, we want to play again, prove our form and get selected for everything. This is how our mind works. On hindsight, I should have come back to play only after getting my best rhythm."

Article Title: USA cricketer Akhilesh Reddy handed 8-year ban by ICC for corruption offences
Article Text:
Akhilesh Reddy

How the case unfolded

USA cricketer Bodugum Akhilesh Reddy has been banned from all forms of cricket for eight years after being found guilty of breaching the International Cricket Council's (ICC) Anti-Corruption Code.According to a press release from the ICC, the 26-year-old's punishment is linked to corruption during the 2025 Abu Dhabi T10 tournament in the UAE. The ban has been backdated to November 21, 2025, when he was provisionally suspended.The ICC, which was overseeing anti-corruption matters for the tournament on behalf of the Emirates Cricket Board, found him guilty on three counts.According to the ICC, Reddy violated: “Article 2.1.1: Attempting to fix, contrive or otherwise influence improperly, or being party to an agreement or effort to fix or contrive in any way or otherwise influence improperly, the result, progress, conduct or other aspect of matches in the ADT10 2025.“Article 2.1.4: Soliciting, inducing, enticing, instructing, persuading, encouraging or intentionally facilitating (or attempting to do the former) another Participant to breach Article 2.1.1 of the Code in one or more Matches in the ADT10 2025.“Article 2.4.7: Obstructing the DACO’s investigation through deletion of data and messages from a mobile device which may have been relevant to the DACO’s investigation.”The case relates to an incident on November 19, 2025, before the opening match of the Aspin Stallions. The tribunal found that Reddy approached a teammate, identified as 'Player A', and asked him to "give runs" while bowling, allegedly on the instructions of team management.After the teammate refused and reported the approach to the ICC Anti-Corruption Unit, he was dropped from the playing XI. Investigators also found that Reddy deleted WhatsApp chats and call logs with the player before the probe. Although he claimed it was routine "data hygiene," the tribunal ruled that he had deliberately destroyed evidence.Reddy has played four T20Is for the USA, claiming one wicket. The verdict was delivered by a three-member ICC Anti-Corruption Tribunal.

There was a time when Auqib Nabi didn't own a pair of bowling spikes.For his first U-19 trial in Jammu & Kashmir, the fast bowler from Baramulla borrowed a pair from a friend. When he eventually earned selection, fate threw up another twist. The friend who had lent him the spikes didn't make the squad. Auqib borrowed another pair from him and played his entire first U-19 tournament in borrowed shoes.Today, Auqib is making a name for himself with a skill that many fast bowlers spend years trying to master: the ability to swing the ball both ways. He has now earned his maiden India call-up, with the 29-year-old seamer from Jammu & Kashmir replacing the injured Jasprit Bumrah in India's Test squad for the upcoming tour of Sri Lanka.Nabi has picked up 104 wickets over the last two Ranji Trophy seasons, virtually breaking the selection door down with his performances. He was also part of the India A squad that toured Sri Lanka recently, where he claimed six wickets in two First Class matches.Yet, the road to the Indian dressing room wasn't built in fancy academies or elite fast-bowling programmes. It was shaped by a long journey, borrowed equipment and an obsession with learning."My parents are government school teachers. Initially, they wanted me to focus on studies, which was natural. Cricket wasn't something we had planned. A friend told me about the Under-19 trials. Until then, I didn't even know they were happening," Auqib had told reporters after picking up a five-wicket haul on the opening day of the Delhi vs Jammu & Kashmir Ranji Trophy match at the Arun Jaitley Stadium in November 2025.Like countless youngsters in Kashmir, his cricketing education began with tennis-ball matches. The transition to leather-ball cricket, however, brought a different challenge."The most basic thing a fast bowler needs is a turf wicket," he had said. "Baramulla had turf, but you couldn't bowl there wearing spikes. So I had to travel to Srinagar to practice."The one-and-a-half-hour journey from Baramulla to Srinagar became part of his routine. Hours on the road simply to bowl a few overs on a proper surface. For many aspiring cricketers, inadequate facilities become a convenient excuse. Auqib never allowed himself that luxury."If you want to play for India, these things cannot become excuses. If you want it badly enough, you have to do it."That philosophy continues to define him.The philosophy kept motivating him day in and day out, but it was his obsession with learning that made him the bowler he is today."When he first joined the J&K team for the Buchi Babu Trophy in Salem in 2023, he could only bowl the outswinger. But he wanted to bowl both ways. So I started working on his inswing," P. Krishnakumar, Jammu & Kashmir's bowling coach, told TimesofIndia.com."He has a great wrist position, which is one of his biggest strengths," he said.There were no shortcuts, and Nabi knew it. He started working on his inswing with Krishnakumar in the nets, and the results began to show in the 2024-25 season."There were a few biomechanical issues as well. I addressed them and rectified them. From the second year, the results started coming. He learnt how to use the ball, how to bowl in the first, second and third sessions. He started identifying batters' weaknesses. He worked on his preparation. Last season he came all guns blazing and we won the Ranji Trophy," he said.The inswing eventually became his biggest weapon. Later, he added the scrambled seam delivery to his arsenal, making himself a far more complete bowler than the one Krishnakumar first saw in Salem.Interestingly, Auqib says the biggest transformation wasn't technical."I have changed my mindset more than anything else. Earlier, I used to think only about taking wickets. Now I just focus on bowling in good areas. Whether the ball swings in or away, my job is to keep hitting the right length," he said.That change has also altered how he views difficult bowling conditions. Flat Indian pitches often test the patience of fast bowlers. Rather than searching for magic deliveries, Auqib has learned to trust the basics."Whether it's the new ball or the old ball, your basics have to stay strong. You have to keep bowling in good areas."His domestic performances did not go unnoticed. He earned an Indian Premier League (IPL) contract worth Rs 8.40 crore with the Delhi Capitals. However, his first IPL season did not go according to plan as he failed to take a single wicket in five matches.But he already knows how he wants to use the money he earned from the IPL. He plans to build an academy in Baramulla."I'd like to open an academy," Nabi had earlier told TimesofIndia.com. "There's absolutely nothing here. When I started playing, I had to go to Bengaluru for training and play lower-division matches there. I want to find and train more Auqib Nabis from Baramulla."Now, with an India call-up, Nabi has added another feather to his cap.Borrowed spikes taught him gratitude. Long journeys taught him perseverance. His obsession with learning the inswing taught him that improvement rarely comes overnight. Together, they have shaped a fast bowler who believes the path to bigger dreams isn't built on excuses or shortcuts, but on showing up every day and bowling one good ball after another.

Article Title: CWG para champions complain against IOA staff, seek action over alleged 'misconduct, disrespectful behaviour'
Article Text:
Dilip Mahadu Gavit and Mohammed Basil Morssinganakathi. (PTI Photo)

NEW DELHI: Fresh from scripting history at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, India’s men’s T47 100m gold and silver medallists Dilip Mahadu Gavit and Mohammed Basil Morssinganakathi have lodged formal complaints with the sports ministry and the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) against an IOA media committee member, alleging rude and disrespectful behaviour towards the country’s para athletes.The complaints have been filed separately by Gavit, Basil and para athletics coach Pushpa NP, who was part of the Indian contingent in Glasgow. It is learnt that Paralympic Committee of India (PCI) CEO Rahul Swami has also submitted a similar complaint to the ministry and the IOA.According to sources, the complaints name Sarvesh Kedia, an IOA media committee member who travelled to Glasgow as one of the Indian contingent’s press attaches and was attached to the chef-de-mission’s office. Kedia was among the 14 IOA officials accompanying India’s combined able-bodied and para athletes’ contingent.In a complaint accessed by TOI, Pushpa alleged that Kedia “was talking loudly with our medal winners Dilip Gavit and Basil and coaches” and said the incident involved him and chief para athletics coach Satyanarayana. She urged the authorities to ensure that Kedia “is not involved in any para athletics media interaction” in future and sought appropriate action against him.The alleged incident took place on July 30 after Gavit clocked 10.71 seconds — a Games record — to become India’s first male para athlete to win a Commonwealth Games athletics gold medal. Basil followed with a season-best of 10.83 seconds to claim silver as India completed a historic 1-2 finish in the men’s T47 100m final.According to sources, a heated argument broke out between Kedia and Satyanarayana over facilitating the athletes’ media interactions before they proceeded for mandatory dope-control procedures. The exchange allegedly escalated into a brief physical altercation before coaches and athletes stepped in to defuse the situation.The incident reportedly left several members of the para athletics contingent deeply upset, prompting the athletes, coaches and PCI officials to submit formal complaints to the sports ministry and the IOA seeking action.
Article Summary: Dilip Mahadu Gavit and Mohammed Basil Morssinganakathi have lodged formal complaints with the sports ministry and the Indian Olympic Association. They allege rude and disrespectful behaviour towards the country’s para athletes. The complaints name Sarvesh Kedia, an IOA media committee member.

Article Title: Food poisoning denied me Commonwealth Games gold, says Selva Prabhu after winning bronze
Article Text:
India's Selva Prabhu Thirumaran competes in the men's triple jump final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland.

Commonwealth Games bronze medallist Selva Prabhu believes food poisoning cost him a chance to win gold in Glasgow, saying a jump close to his personal best would have been enough to finish on top of the podium.Selva won bronze in the men's triple jump with a best effort of 16.52m, finishing behind fellow Indian Praveen Chithravel (16.58m) and Scotland's Jordon Scott (16.72m)."I wish I should have gotten that gold. I was really hoping for gold but what can be done when the competition begins, there is illness and food poisoning. I feel that in the end, there is always a cost to yourself. I am mentally tough so I decided, whatever happens, I will do it. Keep pushing myself," Selva told news agency PTI after returning from Glasgow on Monday.The Tamil Nadu athlete said the illness affected his performance and felt he missed a good opportunity, as a jump close to his personal best of 17.05m would have been enough to win the event."I should have stayed healthy, but it's for the next time I'm always ready. I can compete more, stay healthy. It's about the stage. I have the consistency.It's all about that particular day. I just always want to stay healthy. Now, I want to work on my approach. Once I get the hang of it, I can do it," he said.When asked about the upcoming Asian Games, Selva said his focus remains on taking one step at a time."I live each day. Each day requires a new performance. You just cannot target a gold like that. Yes, I am now looking forward to qualifying for the Asian Games first and then taking it from there," he said.The Athletics Federation of India (AFI) is yet to announce the Indian team for the Asian Games in Japan.

Article Title: CWG 2026: Glasgow restaurant deletes Instagram account after Lovlina Borgohain flags 'incorrect map' of India

NEW DELHI: A Glasgow-based Indian restaurant deleted its Instagram account after Olympic medallist Lovlina Borgohain pointed out that its logo and napkins showed an incorrect map of India.The incident happened after the Indian boxing team visited Mister Singh's India - The Home of Curry to celebrate its historic Commonwealth Games 2026 campaign. India finished with a record 10 boxing medals - seven gold and three silver.During the dinner, Lovlina noticed that the map printed on the restaurant's napkins and displayed outside the restaurant did not include India's Northeast.A video of her raising the issue went viral on social media and drew criticism from many users.Lovlina, who is from Assam and won a silver medal in Glasgow, politely raised the issue with the restaurant management."Please don't take this the wrong way. I felt a little hurt by this. In the map of India, our North East is missing. Yes, even outside, the map that's displayed has cut off the North East. As someone from the North East, that really hurts us. That's all I wanted to say. Please keep this in mind next time. Thank you so much."Soon after the video surfaced, the restaurant issued a public apology and accepted its mistake. It also said the logo would be changed."Mr Singh's India, is very proud of our Indian heritage and ancestry, for almost 32 years we have served, for India and around the world.""First and foremost, we would like to unequivocally apologise for the depiction of the wrong map of India. We will take immediate steps to correct this. Once again our sincere apologies, we never wanted to offend anyone rather wanted to serve with pride to Indian contingent."The restaurant also thanked the Indian team for visiting after their successful campaign."We will change the logo with proper map. It was our humble privilege and honour, that we served team India, after their fantastic, achievements in the Commonwealth Games. All athletes and guests thoroughly enjoyed their evening, these memories will last with us for India. Team Mr Singh India."Shortly after issuing the apology, the restaurant's Instagram account was deleted.Boxing Federation of India president Ajay Singh, who was present at the restaurant, said the matter was handled peacefully."There was no confrontation. It was an aberration and we pointed that out, me and Lovlina. They accepted their mistake and assured us that it will be corrected," Singh told PTI.The restaurant has hosted several visiting sports teams and dignitaries over the years.

LUCKNOW: Asmita Dey took loans to fund her training in Germany ahead of the Commonwealth Games, which bore rich fruit as she became the first Indian judoka to win a gold medal at the Games in Glasgow. Even as she savours the historic feat, the Uttar Pradesh Police sub-inspector has already set her sights on the Asian Games , scheduled to be held in Japan in Sept.However, a lack of funds for overseas training ahead of the big event is threatening to derail her preparations. Speaking to TOI, Asmita said the Asian Games are her next target, but financial constraints have emerged as a major hurdle.“After winning the gold medal at the Commonwealth Games, my focus is now on the Asian Games. I want to go abroad for special training. I am planning to attend a training programme in Valencia, Spain, from Aug 17 to 22, where many international players and coaches will be present. After that, I want to train in Japan before the Asian Games. But I do not have the funds,” Asmita said.“Before the Commonwealth Games, I took a loan for a special training camp in Germany from May to June. I also take care of all my family's expenses,” she added.Asmita, who hails from Tripura, said her judo journey began at the Tripura Sports School, where she studied from Class 7 to Class 10. In 2019, she joined the Sports Authority of India (SAI) centre in Bhopal for regular training and national camps. In 2025, she obtained a no-objection certificate from Tripura and joined the Uttar Pradesh Judo Association.She said her job in the Uttar Pradesh Police has played a crucial role in supporting her sporting career.“I got a job in UP Police as a constable in 2023. That job played a major role in my life. I manage my expenses from my salary. I am very thankful to Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath. When I had nothing, the constable job helped me a lot. At the time of joining, the chief minister gave me a welcome letter,” Asmita said.Asmita said the first person she wanted to share her Commonwealth Games gold with was her father, who died seven months ago after suffering a brain stroke. A cycle mechanic, he earned around Rs 300 a day and raised the family in a mud house in a small village in Tripura.Uttar Pradesh Judo Association secretary Munawar Anzar said he would request the state sports department to arrange funds for Asmita's international training.

8 of India's 13 Commonwealth Games gold medals have been won by women.

NEW DELHI: India's women emerged as the biggest force behind the country's impressive Commonwealth Games campaign, winning eight of the nation's 13 gold medals and underlining their growing dominance across disciplines. From weightlifting and para athletics to judo and boxing, the women athletes not only contributed significantly to India's medal tally but also defined the country's golden run in Glasgow.The stellar performances reflected the remarkable rise of women's sport in India, with a blend of Olympic champions, established stars and emerging talents delivering on the biggest stage. Olympic silver medallist Mirabai Chanu Saikhom once again showcased her class by adding another CWG title to her illustrious career, while Sharmila Dhankar produced a memorable effort to clinch gold in the women's shot put in para athletics.History was scripted on the judo mat as Asmita Dey became India's first-ever CWG judo gold medallist, adding another milestone to the country's campaign.Indian women's boxing, meanwhile, stamped its authority in spectacular fashion. Sakshi Chaudhary, Preeti Pawar , Jaismine Lamboria, Priya Ghanghas and Arundhati Choudhary all finished atop the podium, highlighting the remarkable depth India has developed in women's boxing over the past decade.Together, the eight champions have powered India's campaign and reinforced the message that Indian women are no longer merely contenders on the international stage but consistent winners capable of dominating elite competitions.Indian Olympic Association (IOA) president Dr P T Usha, herself a trailblazer for generations of Indian sportswomen, hailed the achievements as a reflection of years of dedication and belief."Seeing India's women win eight of our 13 gold medals fills me with immense pride. These achievements are the result of years of dedication by the athletes, their families, coaches and support teams. Every medal tells the story of perseverance and sacrifice. More importantly, these champions are inspiring countless young girls across India to believe that they too can wear the India jersey and succeed on the world stage. That is the true spirit of Nari Shakti," she said.The performances also mirror a wider transformation taking place across the country, where increasing emphasis on women's empowerment has translated into greater opportunities in sport. Improved access to training facilities, stronger athlete support systems and sustained encouragement for girls to pursue competitive sport have helped create an ecosystem in which talent continues to flourish.Beyond the medals, India's women displayed exceptional team spirit throughout the Games, with senior athletes mentoring younger teammates and celebrating each other's successes. Their performances have inspired millions of young girls across the country, proving that sporting excellence knows no gender.The medals will adorn trophy cabinets, and records may eventually be broken, but the inspiration created by Mirabai Chanu, Sharmila Dhankar, Asmita Dey, Sakshi Chaudhary, Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Priya Ghanghas and Arundhati Choudhary promises to leave a lasting legacy.

Article Title: After historic CWG gold, Mirabai Chanu declares Asian Games 'make-or-break'
Article Text:
Mirabai Chanu (Image credit: X)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: There is little left for Saikhom Mirabai Chanu to conquer at the Commonwealth Games.A record-extending third consecutive CWG gold medal in Glasgow has only strengthened her status as the undisputed queen of Commonwealth weightlifting. Add the silver she won in her debut Games in 2014, and Mirabai now stands as the most successful weightlifting athlete in CWG history.Yet, less than 24 hours after standing atop the podium once again, the Tokyo Olympic silver medallist had already turned the page."The very next day after winning gold, I started preparing for the Asian Games . I started training the next day itself," Mirabai told TOI upon her return to India on Sunday afternoon.For the 32-year-old, the celebrations are over. The focus has shifted completely to the one medal that has remained painfully out of reach throughout her glittering career — an Asian Games podium finish."The upcoming Games in Japan are very important for me. I don't have an Asiad medal and I want to win one. Before every Asiad, I have either suffered an injury or something has happened because of which I missed out on a medal.This time I have to overcome that. My focus is purely on the event. That's the one title I desperately want to win," she said.Having carried Indian weightlifting on her shoulders for more than a decade while battling recurring injuries, Mirabai knows opportunities are becoming increasingly precious."I am not thinking whether this will be my last Asiad or not. But I will compete like this is the best opportunity I have to win a medal...like this is the only Asiad I have. Future competitions can wait. Right now, the Aich-Nagoya Games offers me the best chance. For me, it is a make-or-break moment."Those words carry the weight of a career shaped as much by injuries as medals.The build-up to Glasgow was anything but straightforward. Mirabai won gold at the National Championships in Modinagar in Feb, setting national records in the process, but picked up a shoulder injury during the competition. The setback forced her to miss the Asian Championships as she stepped away from competition for months to allow her body to recover.Her comeback, however, was vintage Mirabai.Competing in Glasgow after months away from the platform, she comfortably lifted a Games record total of 190kg — 85kg in snatch and 105kg in clean and jerk — to clinch India's first gold of this edition of the Games. More importantly, she achieved what no other weightlifter has managed before by winning three successive CWG gold.It was the performance of a champion who understood the bigger picture.Mirabai admitted she deliberately avoided exhausting herself in Glasgow, preserving both her body and energy for the much bigger challenge that awaits in Japan."I preserved myself during the CWG. My focus was always on the Asiad. Now I have to improve my performance level. The competition there will be much tougher."That challenge will be formidable. Olympic champion Hou Zhihui of China, the powerful North Korean lifters and Thailand's Surodchana Khambao are likely to headline a world-class field where every kilogram can separate the medal winners from the rest."I have to train harder. China, North Korea and Thailand have very strong weightlifters. I need to raise my performance several notches. I have to prepare more and train harder."Unlike previous major championships, Mirabai will remain in India for the final phase of her preparations under long-time coach Vijay Sharma."There isn't much time before the Games. We cannot go abroad now. I will train here in India under Vijay sir. I will follow the same routine as I do before every major championship. Nothing special, but my performance level has to improve."Years of competing at the highest level have also taught Mirabai to respect her body's limits."I understand my body much better now. I know how my mind and body react. I have learnt from injuries and experience. That understanding is very important."Beyond the Games lies another major transition. With the International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) scrapping the women's 49kg division for the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, Mirabai will eventually have to move up to the new 53kg category — another challenge in an already extraordinary career.But that is a story for another day. For now, India's most decorated Commonwealth weightlifter has only one destination in mind. "This Games is the biggest moment for me. I have to come back with a medal at any cost. I don't want to let this opportunity go."
Article Summary: Saikhom Mirabai Chanu won a record-extending third consecutive CWG gold medal in Glasgow. The 32-year-old now stands as the most successful weightlifting athlete in CWG history. The Tokyo Olympic silver medallist had already turned the page.

Article Title: 'I gave up': Tejaswin Shankar's emotional confession after turning CWG heartbreak into historic bronze
Article Text:
Tejaswin Shankar celebrates after winning the bronze medal in the men's decathlon event. (PTI Photo)

'I questioned everything'



From despair to historic bronze



'Your belief carried me'



Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: There were tears after one jump. Days later, there was history, a medal and a message that resonated far beyond the athletics track.Indian decathlete Tejaswin Shankar has opened up on the emotional turmoil he endured at the 2026 Commonwealth Games, revealing that he briefly "gave up" after a recurring knee injury shattered his hopes in the high jump before he picked himself up to script history with India's first-ever Commonwealth Games medal in the decathlon.The national record holder shared a deeply personal message on social media after returning home with a bronze medal, admitting the journey from heartbreak to the podium was one of the toughest tests of his career."There are moments in life when you feel like everything you've worked for is slipping away. This week, I had one of those moments," Tejaswin wrote.The 27-year-old had travelled to Glasgow hoping to defend the bronze medal he won in the high jump at the Birmingham Commonwealth Games in 2022 — India's first-ever medal in the event.Instead, his campaign unravelled almost instantly.A long-standing battle with chronic patellar tendinitis, commonly known as jumper's knee, resurfaced after his very first attempt in the high jump, forcing him to withdraw from the competition.The sight of Tejaswin crouching alone on the track, struggling to hold back tears, became one of the defining images of India's campaign.Those tears, however, were not because of physical pain."I’m going to be honest and admit for a while, I gave up," he revealed. "I questioned everything. I wondered if all the preparation had been for nothing."For any elite athlete, such moments can define a career. But for Tejaswin, they became the beginning of an extraordinary comeback.Instead of allowing disappointment to consume him, Tejaswin slowly rebuilt himself over the next few days."But somewhere along the way, I picked myself back up piece by piece. I was shattered emotionally but kept lying to myself that I was fine. One conversation, one treatment session, one event, one lap at a time," he added.Competing through pain, the Indian produced a remarkable performance across the gruelling two-day decathlon to finish with 7,976 points and claim the bronze medal — the first ever by an Indian in the event at the Commonwealth Games.It also marked his second Commonwealth Games medal after the high jump bronze in Birmingham four years ago.After clinching the historic podium finish, Tejaswin walked into the mixed zone with a smile replacing the tears seen earlier in the week."Guys, I won't cry today," he joked.The bronze was all the more remarkable considering he had entered the final 1,500m in third place and held on under immense physical and mental pressure to secure the medal.Reflecting on his remarkable turnaround, Tejaswin credited the people around him for helping him rediscover belief when he had lost faith in himself."Looking back, I realize I didn't do it alone. To my coaches, medical team, teammates, family, friends, sponsors, and every single person who called, messaged, or reached out on social media… thank you. Your belief carried me when I was struggling very hard to believe in myself," he wrote.The athlete also reflected on the deeper lessons sport continues to teach."Sport has a funny way of testing you. Sometimes it isn't about being the strongest or the most talented. Sometimes it's simply about refusing to stay down.""Proud to leave the Commonwealth Games with a bronze medal around my neck. It wasn't the path I imagined, but it taught me more than an easy victory ever could," he added.With Glasgow behind him, Tejaswin has already shifted his focus to the next challenge. Asian Games , see you soon. The Beast Never Stops," he concluded.
Article Summary: Indian decathlete Tejaswin Shankar has opened up on the emotional turmoil he endured at the 2026 Commonwealth Games. The 27-year-old revealed that he briefly "gave up" after a recurring knee injury shattered his hopes in the high jump. But he picked himself up to script history with India's first-ever Commonwealth Games medal in the decathlon.

Article Title: CWG 2026: Smiling the best defence for boxer Arundhati Chaudhary
Article Text:
Arundhati Chaudhary (Image credit: X)

Ever seen a boxer smile while landing punches and taking jabs on the chin? That’s Arundhati Chaudhary for you. The Kota boxer, who won gold in the women’s 70kg event at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow on Saturday, smiles throughout her bout. The boxer says smiling is her defence mechanism, but it also often rattles the opponent’s confidence.“Our training sessions are so intense that our heart rate hits 208bpm. It’s exhausting, extremely hot, and frustrating, so all the crying and anger happen during training. Those moments in the ring are what we work so hard for 365 days a year. Those nine minutes in the ring are the best time to enjoy, and I consider them the best moments of my life.”Arundhati hails from Kota, a place in Rajasthan that is known for making good IITians (and maybe kachoris), but boxers, none.“I used to play basketball in school, but my parents wanted me to quit sports after the 10th standard and prepare for the IIT entrance exams. But I told my father, ‘how many people clear IIT every year, and how many of their names do you actually remember? But if I bring home an Olympic medal, even long after I am gone, people will still remember my name’.That worked,” Arundhati recalled.Finding a boxing coach in Kota was more difficult than even pursuing the sport.“My parents searched everywhere, from Bharatpur to Jaipur, Rohtak and Bhopal, but they weren’t comfortable sending a 15-year-old girl away on her own. Eventually, a local coach in Kota, Ashok Gautam sir, agreed to train me. He was a wushu coach who learned boxing techniques from YouTube and then taught me.”Two years after taking up boxing, Arundhati faced a life-threatening injury in 2018. While participating a practice bout with a male boxer, she was punched in the head.“I suffered a blood clot in my brain, after taking foul punches. I collapsed, lost memory, and doctors warned that continuing boxing would be life-threatening. My mother pleaded with my father to stop me, but I was adamant. My father ultimately stood by my decision.”

Indian cyclist Harshita Jakhar created history by becoming the first Indian woman to be part of the Tour de France Femmes.The 19-year-old rode alongside seven other young cyclists from Afghanistan, Algeria, Chile, Ethiopia, Namibia and Uganda during the ceremonial start of Stage 2 on Sunday.The group, selected by the Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI), completed a 4.5-km neutralised section of the course before the professional riders began the stage.
